section.heading: 6.1. Areas between Curves
section.paragraph: In Chapter 5 we defined and calculated areas of regions that lie under the graphs of functions. Here we use integrals to find areas of regions that lie between the graphs of two functions.
section.heading: Area between Curves: Integrating with Respect to x
section.paragraph: Consider the region $$S$$ shown in Figure 1 that lies between two curves $$y = f{(x)}$$ and $$y = g{(x)}$$ and between the vertical lines $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ , where $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous functions and $$f{(x)} \geqslant g{(x)}$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .

image.alt: Details Two curves, two line segments, and a shaded region are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. There are two tick marks on the x axis, with a to the right of the origin, and b to the right of a. The second curve, labeled y = g(x), begins in the fourth quadrant, down and to the right of the origin, goes down to the right, concave up, and then goes up to the right, concave down, crosses the positive x axis and then the curve f(x). The second line segment is to the right of the first line, rises vertically upward from x = b, and crosses the second curve, and meets the first curve y = f(x). The region bound by the two curves between the two line segments is shaded and labeled S.

section.paragraph: Just as we did for areas under curves in Section 5.1, we divide $$S$$ into $$n$$ strips of equal width and then we approximate the $$i$$ th strip by a rectangle with base $$\Delta x$$ and height $$f{(x_{i}^{\ast})} - g{(x_{i}^{\ast})}$$ . (See Figure 2. If we like, we could take all of the sample points to be right endpoints, in which case $$x_{i}^{\ast} = x_{i}$$ .) The Riemann sum
$$\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{{\lbrack{f{(x_{i}^{*})} - g{(x_{i}^{*})}}\rbrack}\Delta x}$$
is therefore an approximation to what we intuitively think of as the area of $$S$$ .

section.paragraph: This approximation appears to become better and better as $$\left. n\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ . Therefore we define the area $$A$$ of the region $$S$$ as the limiting value of the sum of the areas of these approximating rectangles.
$$A = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}\lbrack f(x_{i}^{*}) - g(x_{i}^{*})\rbrack\Delta x$$
We recognize the limit in (1) as the definite integral of $$f - g$$ . Therefore we have the following formula for area.

The area $$A$$ of the region bounded by the curves $$y = f(x)$$ , $$y = g(x)$$ , and the lines $$x = a$$ , $$x = b$$ , where $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous and $$f(x) \geqslant g(x)$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , is
$$A = \int_{a}^{b}\lbrack f(x) - g(x)\rbrack dx$$
Notice that in the special case where $$g(x) = 0$$ , $$S$$ is the region under the graph of $$f$$ and our general definition of area (1) reduces to our previous definition (Definition 5.1.2).
In the case where both $$f$$ and $$g$$ are positive, you can see from Figure 3 why (2) is true:

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\lbrack{{area under}y = f{(x)}}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{{area under}y = g{(x)}}\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{a}^{b}{f{(x)}dx -}}\int_{a}^{b}g{(x)}dx = \int_{a}^{b}\lbrack f(x) - g(x)\rbrack dx} \end{array}$$

There are two tick marks on the x axis, with a to the right of the origin, and b to the right of a. The second line rises vertically upward from x = b to meet the meeting point of both the curves. The area below y = f(x), bound by the two lines is shaded. example.paragraph: Find the area of the region bounded above by $$y = e^{ x}$$ , bounded below by $$y = x$$ , and bounded on the sides by $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ .

section.paragraph: In Figure 4 we drew a typical approximating rectangle with width $$\Delta x$$ as a reminder of the procedure by which the area is defined in (1). In general, when we set up an integral for an area, it’s helpful to sketch the region to identify the top curve $$y_{T}$$ , the bottom curve $$y_{B}$$ , and a typical approximating rectangle as in Figure 5. Then the area of a typical rectangle is $${({y_{T} - y_{B}})}\Delta x$$ and the equation
$$A = \lim\limits_{n\rightarrow\infty}\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{n}{{\left( {y_{T} - y_{B}} \right)}\Delta x} = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left( {y_{T} - y_{B}} \right)dx}}$$
summarizes the procedure of adding (in a limiting sense) the areas of all the typical rectangles.

The area within the rectangle is shaded darker.

section.paragraph: Notice that in Figure 5 the left-hand boundary reduces to a point, whereas in Figure 3 the right-hand boundary reduces to a point. In the next example both of the side boundaries reduce to a point, so the first step is to find $$a$$ and $$b$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find the area of the region enclosed by the parabolas $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$y = 2x - x^{2}$$ .

Solution We first find the points of intersection of the parabolas by solving their equations simultaneously. This gives $$x^{2} = 2x - x^{2}$$ , or $$2x^{2} - 2x = 0$$ . Thus $$2x\left( {x - 1} \right) = 0$$ , so $$x = 0$$ or $$1$$ . The points of intersection are $$(0,0)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ .
We see from Figure 6 that the top and bottom boundaries are
and
The area of a typical rectangle is
$${({y_{T} - y_{B}})}\Delta x = {\left( {2x - x^{2} - x^{2}} \right)}\Delta x = \left( {\left. 2x - 2x^{2} \right)\Delta x} \right.$$
and the region lies between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ . So the total area is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {2x - 2x^{2}} \right)dx = 2}}{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {x - x^{2}} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = 2\left\lbrack {\frac{x^{2}}{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} = 2\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}} \right) = \frac{1}{3}} \end{array}$$

A dashed line segment connects the mid points of the top and bottom sides. The area within the rectangle is shaded darker.

section.paragraph: Sometimes it’s difficult, or even impossible, to find the points of intersection of two curves exactly. As shown in the following example, we can use a graphing calculator or computer to find approximate values for the intersection points and then proceed as before.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Find the approximate area of the region bounded by the curves $$y = x \slash \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$ and $$y = x^{4} - x$$ .
Solution If we were to try to find the exact intersection points, we would have to solve the equation

This looks like a very difficult equation to solve exactly (in fact, it’s impossible), so instead we graph the two curves using a computer (see Figure 7). One intersection point is the origin, and we find that the other occurs when $$x \approx 1.18$$ . So an approximation to the area between the curves is
$$A \approx {\int_{0}^{1.18}{{\left\lbrack {\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} - {({x^{4} - x})}} \right\rbrack}dx}}$$
To integrate the first term we use the substitution $$u = x^{2} + 1$$ . Then $$du = 2xdx$$ , and when $$x = 1.18$$ , we have $$u \approx 2.39$$ ; when $$x = 0$$ , $$u = 1$$ . So

$$\begin{array}{l} {A \approx {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{1}^{2.39}{\frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} - {\int_{0}^{1.18}{{({x^{4} - x})}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. \sqrt{u} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2.39} - \left\lbrack {\frac{x^{5}}{5} - \frac{x^{2}}{2}} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1.18}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\sqrt{2.39} - 1 - \frac{(1.18)^{5}}{5} + \frac{(1.18)^{2}}{2}}} \\ {\phantom{A} \approx 0.785} \end{array}$$

The horizontal axis ranges from negative 1 to 2 and the vertical axis from negative 1 to 1.5, both in increments of 0.5. The first curve, y = x^4 minus x enters from the top left corner of the viewing window, goes down to the right, concave up, gradually at first, and then more steeply and almost linearly, crosses the origin, reaches a low point at approximately (0.6, negative 0.5), goes up to the right, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), and exits the window at approximately (1.25, 1.5). The second curve, labeled y = x/sqrt(x^1 + 1), enters the viewing window slightly above the bottom left corner, goes up to the right, concave up, becomes concave down as it crosses the first curve at the origin, more and more gradually, crosses the first curve again at approximately (1.25, 0.75) and exits the viewing window at approximately (2, 1). The region bound by the two curves is shaded.

section.paragraph: If we are asked to find the area between the curves $$y = f(x)$$ and $$y = g(x)$$ where $$f(x) \geqslant g(x)$$ for some values of $$x$$ but $$g(x) \geqslant f(x)$$ for other values of $$x$$ , then we split the given region $$S$$ into several regions $$S_{1},S_{2},\ldots$$ with areas $$A_{1},A_{2},\ldots$$ as shown in Figure 8. We then define the area of the region $$S$$ to be the sum of the areas of the smaller regions $$S_{1},S_{2},\ldots$$ , that is, $$A = A_{1} + A_{2} + \cdots$$ . Since
$$|f(x) - g(x)| = \left\{ \begin{array}{l} {f(x) - g(x) \text{when} f(x) \geqslant g(x)} \\ {g(x) - f(x) \text{when} g(x) \geqslant f(x)} \end{array} \right.$$
we have the following expression for $$A$$ .
The area between the curves $$y = f(x)$$ and $$y = g(x)$$ and between $$x = a$$ and $$x = b$$ is

The first curve, y = f(x), begins from directly above x = a, goes up to the right, concave down, reaches a high point, goes down to the right, initially concave down and then concave up, reaches a low point, goes up to the right, initially concave up and then concave down and ends directly above x = b. The second curve, labeled y = g(x), also begins directly above x = a, gradually goes up to the right, concave down, crosses the first curve just before it inflects, reaches a high point, goes down to the right, crossing the first curve again just as it inflicts again, and ends directly above x = b. Another region bound only by the two curves lies between S_1 and S_3 and is labeled S_2. This region is shaded with a different color.

section.paragraph: When evaluating the integral in (3), however, we must still split it into integrals corresponding to $$A_{1},A_{2},\ldots$$ .

Solution The points of intersection occur when $$\sin x = \cos x$$ , that is, when $$x = \pi \slash 4$$ (since $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ ). The region is sketched in Figure 9.

example.paragraph: Observe that $$\cos x \geqslant \sin x$$ when $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 4$$ but $$\sin x \geqslant \cos x$$ when $$\pi \slash 4 \leqslant x \leqslant \pi \slash 2$$ . Therefore the required area is

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 2}\left| \cos x - \sin x \middle| dx = A_{1} + A_{2} \right.}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{0}^{\pi \slash 4}{{({\cos x - \sin x})}dx + {\int_{\pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 2}{{({\sin x - \cos x})}dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\left\lbrack {\sin x + \cos x} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi \slash 4} + \left\lbrack {- \cos x - \sin x} \right\rbrack_{\pi \slash 4}^{\pi \slash 2}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\left( {\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 0 - 1} \right) + \left( {- 0 - 1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {2\sqrt{2} - 2}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Area between Curves: Integrating with Respect to y
section.paragraph: Some regions are best treated by regarding $$x$$ as a function of $$y$$ . If a region is bounded by curves with equations $$x = f(y)$$ , $$x = g(y)$$ , $$y = c$$ , and $$y = d$$ , where $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous and $$f(y) \geqslant g(y)$$ for $$c \leqslant y \leqslant d$$ (See Figure 10), then its area is
$$A = {\int_{c}^{d}{{\lbrack{f{(y)} - g{(y)}}\rbrack}dy}}$$

The y axis has two tick marks, c and d, with c below d. The first curve, labeled x = f(y), is to the right of the viewing window, begins directly across the tick mark d on the y axis, goes down rapidly to the right, bulging rightward. The second curve, x = g(y), is to the left of the first curve, also begins directly across y = d, goes down rapidly to the right, initially briefly bulging to the right and then bulges to the left. The region bound by the two curves and the two line segments is shaded. The area within the rectangle is shaded darker. A dashed line segment connects the mid points of the left and right side of the rectangle.

section.paragraph: If we write $$x_{R}$$ for the right boundary and $$x_{L}$$ for the left boundary, then, as Figure 11 illustrates, we have
$$A = {\int_{c}^{d}{{\left( {x_{R} - x_{L}} \right)}dy}}$$
Here a typical approximating rectangle has dimensions $$x_{R} - x_{L}$$ and $$\Delta y$$ .

The area within the rectangle is shaded darker.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the area enclosed by the line $$y = x - 1$$ and the parabola $$y^{2} = 2x + 6$$ .

Solution By solving the two equations simultaneously we find that the points of intersection are $$\left( {- 1, - 2} \right)$$ and $$\left( {5,4} \right)$$ . We solve the equation of the parabola for $$x$$ and notice from Figure 12 that the left and right boundary curves are
and
We must integrate between the appropriate $$y$$ -values, $$y = - 2$$ and $$y = 4$$ . Thus

$$\begin{array}{l} {A = {{\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {x_{R} - x_{L}} \right)}dy}} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{\left\lbrack {\left( {y + 1} \right) - \left( {\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - 3} \right)} \right\rbrack dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{- 2}^{4}{{\left( {- \frac{1}{2}y^{2} + y + 4} \right)}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. {- \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{y^{3}}{3} \right) + \frac{y^{2}}{2} + 4y} \right\rbrack_{- 2}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {- \frac{1}{6}(64) + 8 + 16 - \left( {\frac{4}{3} + 2 - 8} \right) = 18}} \end{array}$$

Because the bottom boundary consists of two different curves, it would have meant splitting the region in two and computing the areas labeled $$A_{1}$$ and $$A_{2}$$ in Figure 13. The method we used in Example 5 is much easier.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find the area of the region enclosed by the curves $$y = 1/x$$ , $$y = x$$ , and $$y = \frac{1}{4}x$$ , using

list.item: If we integrate with respect to $$x$$ , we must split the region into two parts because the top boundary consists of two separate curves, as shown in Figure 15(a). We compute the area as $$\begin{array}{l} {A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \int_{0}^{1}(x - \frac{1}{4}x)\mathit{dx} + \int_{1}^{2}\left( \frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{4}x \right)\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left\lbrack \frac{3}{8}x^{2} \right\rbrack_{0}^{1} + \left\lbrack \ln x - \frac{1}{8}x^{2} \right\rbrack_{1}^{2} = \ln 2} \end{array}$$

If we integrate with respect to $$y$$ , we also need to divide the region into two parts because the right boundary consists of two separate curves, as shown in Figure 15(b). section.heading: Applications

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Figure 16 shows velocity curves for two cars, A and B, that start side by side and move along the same road. What does the area between the curves represent? Use the Midpoint Rule to estimate it.

image.alt: Details Two curves are graphed on the first coordinate of a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis is labeled t and displayed from 0 to 16 in increments of 2. The vertical axis is labeled v and displayed from 0 to 60 in increments of 10. Both the curves begin at the origin, go upward to the right, and concave down, rapidly at first, and then gradually. The curves are very similar. The top curve is labeled A and above the bottom, a curve is labeled B. Curve A passes through the points (1, 15), (6, 45), and (9, 55) and ends at (16, 65). Curve B passes through the points (6, 30), (11, 4), and ends at (16, 45).

example.paragraph: Solution We know from Section 5.4 that the area under the velocity curve $$A$$ represents the distance traveled by car A during the first $$16$$ seconds. Similarly, the area under curve $$B$$ is the distance traveled by car B during that time period. So the area between these curves, which is the difference of the areas under the curves, is the distance between the cars after $$16$$ seconds. We read the velocities from the graph and convert them to feet per second $$({1{mi} \slash h = \frac{5280}{3600}{ft} \slash s})$$ .

We use the Midpoint Rule with $$n = 4$$ intervals, so that $$\Delta t = 4$$ . The midpoints of the intervals are $${\overline{t}}_{1} = 2$$ , $${\overline{t}}_{2} = 6$$ , $${\overline{t}}_{3} = 10$$ , and $${\overline{t}}_{4} = 14$$ . We estimate the distance between the cars after $$16$$ seconds as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{0}^{16}{\left( {\upsilon_{A} - \upsilon_{B}} \right)}dt \approx \Delta t\left\lbrack {13 + 23 + 28 + 29} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{16}{\left( {\upsilon_{A} - \upsilon_{B}} \right)}dt} = 4(93) = 372{ft}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Figure 17 is an example of a pathogenesis curve for a measles infection. It shows how the disease develops in an individual with no immunity after the measles virus spreads to the bloodstream from the respiratory tract.

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The vertical axis is labeled N, labeled the Number of infected cells per milliliter of blood plasma, and is displayed from 0 to 1500 in increments of 500. The horizontal axis is labeled t (days) and has the tick marks labeled 0: Pathogen enters plasma, 10 to 11: Infectiousness begins, 12: Symptoms appear, 17 to 18: Infectiousness ends, and 21: Pathogen is cleared, from left to right. The curve begins from the origin, goes up to the right, gradually at first and then more rapidly, reaches a peak at approximately (15, 1500), descends rapidly, and meets the horizontal axis at the tick mark 21.

example.paragraph: The patient becomes infectious to others once the concentration of infected cells becomes great enough and remains infectious until the immune system manages to prevent further transmission. However, symptoms don’t develop until the “amount of infection” reaches a particular threshold. The amount of infection needed to develop symptoms depends on both the concentration of infected cells and time, and corresponds to the area under the pathogenesis curve until symptoms appear. (See Exercise 5.1.15.)

(a) The pathogenesis curve in Figure 17 has been modeled by $$f(t) = - t\left( {t - 21} \right)\left( {t + 1} \right)$$ . If infectiousness begins on day $$t_{1} = 10$$ and ends on day $$t_{2} = 18$$ , what are the corresponding concentration levels of infected cells?

(b) The level of infectiousness for an infected person is the area between $$N = f(t)$$ and the line through the points $$P_{1}\left( {t_{1},f\left( t_{1} \right)} \right)$$ and $$P_{2}\left( {t_{2},f\left( t_{2} \right)} \right)$$ , measured in $$({cells} \slash {mL}) \cdot {days}$$ . (See Figure 18.) Compute the level of infectiousness for this particular patient.

image.alt: Details A curve, three line segments, and a shaded region are graphed on the first quadrant of a coordinate plane. The vertical axis is labeled N and is unmarked. The horizontal axis is labeled t (days) and has two tick marks: 10 and 18. The curve labeled f, begins from the origin, goes up to the right, reaches a peak between marks 10 and 18, and then goes down to the right steeply meeting the horizontal axis to the right of the tick mark 18. From the tick marks 10 and 18 on the horizontal axis, vertical line segments rise vertically upward to meet the curve at marked points P_1 and P_2, with P_1 higher than P_2. A line segment connects the points P_1 and P_2. The region is bound by the line segment connecting P_1 and P_2 and the peak of the curve is shaded.

example.paragraph: Solution
(a) Infectiousness begins when the concentration reaches $$f(10) = 1210{cells} \slash {mL}$$ and ends when the concentration reduces to $$f(18) = 1026{cells} \slash {mL}$$ .

(b) The line through $$P_{1}$$ and $$P_{2}$$ has slope $$\frac{1026 - 1210}{18 - 10} = - \frac{184}{8} = - 23$$ and equation $$\left. N - 1210 = - 23\left( {t - 10} \right)\Leftrightarrow N = - 23t + 1440 \right.$$ . The area between $$f$$ and this line is
Thus the level of infectiousness for this patient is about $$1877({cells} \slash {mL}) \cdot {days}$$ .

section.heading: Applied Project The Gini Index
section.paragraph: How is it possible to measure the distribution of income among the inhabitants of a given country? One such measure is the Gini index, named after the Italian economist Corrado Gini, who first devised it in 1912.

We first rank all households in a country by income and then we compute the percentage of households whose total income is a given percentage of the country’s total income. We define a Lorenz curve $$y = L(x)$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ by plotting the point $$\left( {a \slash 100,b \slash 100} \right)$$ on the curve if the bottom $$a\%$$ of households receive $$b\%$$ of the total income. For instance, in Figure 1 the point $$\left( {0.4,0.114} \right)$$ is on the Lorenz curve for the United States in 2016 because the poorest $$40\%$$ of the population received just $$48.5\%$$ of the total income. Likewise, the bottom $$80\%$$ of the population received $$11.4\%$$ of the total income, so the point $$\left( {0.8,0.485} \right)$$ lies on the Lorenz curve. (The Lorenz curve is named after the American economist Max Lorenz.)

image.alt: Details A curve and two points are graphed on the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is marked displayed from 0 to 1 in increments of 0.2 and the y axis is displayed from 0 to 1 in increments of 1. The curve begins at the origin, goes up to the right, concave up, and exits at the top right of the viewing window. The curve passes through two marked points labeled (0.4, 0.114) and (0.8, 0.485).

figure.caption: Lorenz curve for the United States in 2016

section.paragraph: Figure 2 shows some typical Lorenz curves. They all pass through the points $$(0,0)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and are concave upward. In the extreme case $$L(x) = x$$ , society is perfectly egalitarian: the poorest $$a\%$$ of the population receives $$a\%$$ of the total income and so everybody receives the same income. The area between a Lorenz curve $$y = L(x)$$ and the line $$y = x$$ measures how much the income distribution differs from absolute equality. The Gini index (sometimes called the Gini coefficient or the coefficient of inequality) is the area between the Lorenz curve and the line $$y = x$$ (shaded in Figure 3) divided by the area under $$y = x$$ .

The second curve, directly below the first one, briefly runs along the x axis and then goes up to the right, concave up, until (1, 1). The third curve, directly below the second, runs along the x axis further than the second curve and then rapidly goes up to the right, concave up until (1, 1).
